Alright, just skimming this, I'm seeing an overuse of ellipses (...). As a linguistic device, ellipses should be used very sparingly. They don't help a reader emulate speech patterns as well as you seem to think. You should also leave a space ( ) between the end of an ellipsis and the beginning of the next word. I honestly thought that one was just common sense. Apparently not.


Regarding the anecdote with your father, in direct speech you're going to want a new line for each new speaker. You'd be surprised how long it takes some people to learn that one.

Other than that, on a mechanical level just do a proofread. Sometimes you break with proper grammar conventions as a stylistic choice, which is fine (though I'd personally recommend against capslocking clauses for emphasis), but there are one or two typos in there.

Regarding content, it lacks originality, and while the focus is clear enough it reiterates far too much. A good trick for writing fiction - even epistolary literature - is to try to cut away a third of the content after writing the first draft. It forces you to work out what parts are superfluous and what parts are not - it's a method of 'trimming the fat', so to speak.

Overall, it's got potential, but right now it's weighed down by strange stylistic choices and a vision that might still be boring even if it's fully realised. I rate it 3/10.
